Informed Consent to Participate in Research
Title of Research: TCU Screenomics: Linking Human Digital Phenotyping with Mental Health
Principal Investigator: Dr. Qinxin Shi
Overview

You are invited to participate in a research study. To participate, you must be

1) Able to see and hear clearly
2) Able to speak and read English fluently
3) Living in the United States
4) At least 18 years old, but not older than 25 years old
5) The sole user of an Android smartphone (not shared)
6) Active user of at least 2 social media accounts
Study Details

This study is being conducted online and at the laboratory room 213 at Winton-Scott Hall, at Texas Christian University (TCU), and is supported/sponsored by the TCU new faculty start-up funding. This study is an observational study designed to understand daily digital behaviors among young adults (ages 18–22) using multimodal passive sensing markers combining both physiological signals and smartphone screenshots and brief self-report surveys to understand the emergence of mental health symptoms.

Mental health has become a significant global challenge. Rates of mental health symptoms among U.S. young adults have surged to unprecedented levels over the past decade, with approximately one in five reporting recent symptoms of anxiety (35.5%) or depression (26.9%). This increase has been especially pronounced among Generation Z. However, over 50% experiencing mental health symptoms have never received a timely diagnosis or intervention. Traditional diagnostic approaches rely primarily on labor-intensive clinical interviews and retrospective self-report questionnaires, which are constrained by subjectivity and recall biases, infrequent assessment, and limited ecological validity. Moreover, traditional face-to-face interventions are based on scheduled, clinic-based care and one-size-fits-all models, limiting the detection of personalized and moment-to-moment mental health symptom fluctuations as they emerge in real-time, naturalistic settings.

With the proliferation of digital health technologies, wearable-based passive sensing (e.g., Garmin, Fitbit) has emerged as a promising marker for early detection of mental health symptoms, by continuously capturing physiological signals such as heart rate, respiratory rate, movements, stress level, and sleep. For young adults, who spend an average of 6.67 hours per day on non-educational social media, their social media use serves as additional passive sensing markers for detecting mental health symptoms beyond physiological signals. Empirical evidence examining associations between young adults' social media use and mental health symptoms remains inconsistent, with studies reporting null, small, or mixed effects. One key reason is that most prior research relies on self-reported time on social media using a cross-sectional design, which is subject to recall bias and measurement inaccuracy and limits our understanding of social media effects over time.

Together, these gaps highlight the urgent need to identify and validate personalized and objective passive sensing markers to support the timely detection of mental health symptoms in young adults. Passively capturing physiological data and smartphone screenshots (i.e., screenome data) offers a low-burden method for real-time and early detection, as well as providing broader, more accurate, temporally sensitive, and ecologically valid passive sensing markers on mental health symptoms than traditional self-reports.

Participants are asked to install a smartphone application (Screenomics) that passively captures screenshots approximately every five seconds while the phone is in use, as well as a second application (Centralive) used to complete ecological momentary assessment (EMA) surveys approximately four times per day over 28 days. In addition, participants are asked to wear a Garmin wearable device continuously throughout the study period (except during charging). Centralive (Centralive, 2024) is a HIPAA-compliant, code-free, closed-loop mobile health research platform developed to streamline real-world clinical studies (https://centralive.health/#). The Centralive app will be securely linked with the Garmin vívosmart® 5 wearable devices to enable passive collection of physiological data (i.e., heart rate, respiratory rate, movements, stress level, and sleep). Screenomics is an open-source, privacy-aware platform for collecting high-resolution digital life data from study participants' smartphones (https://stanfordscreenomics.github.io/).
Participants

You are being asked to take part because you are an Android user and are within the age range 18-25. If you decide to be in this study, you will be one of 60 participants in this research study at TCU.
Voluntary Participation
Your participation is voluntary. You are not required to participate and may withdraw at any time.
Confidentiality
Even if we publish the findings from this study, we will maintain the confidentiality of your information. Anyone with the authority to look at your records must keep them confidential.
What is the purpose of the research?

The purpose of this study is to understand how young adults use digital devices, and how their daily smartphone habits and body\'s physical signals, such as heart rate, sleep, and activity, are connected to mental health and overall wellbeing. By combining data from wearable devices with a \"Screenomics\" approach (which looks at how you interact with your phone screen), we want to see how these factors work together to influence your well-being in real-time.\n\nWe hope to identify specific digital and physical patterns that signal changes in mood, stress levels, and mental health symptoms. It will help us learn how to detect mental health needs early and provide more personalized support for young adults in the future.
What are the risks of participating in this study, and how will they be minimized?

This study is an observational study with moderate risks, which is higher than minimal. While many aspects of data collection occur passively in the background, participation involves several activities that may introduce time, cognitive, and privacy-related burden, and so psychological and privacy risks. Below, we describe the nature and anticipated magnitude of each source of risk/burden and the steps taken to minimize them.
Psychological Risk – Sensitive Survey Questions:

• Study surveys include questions about mental health symptoms. Although these topics are not clinical in nature, some participants may experience mild discomfort when reflecting on negative emotions, stressful experiences, or other sensitive aspects of their daily lives.

• How we minimize:
 o You can skip any question you don't want to answer and discuss with the study staff by email if something feels uncomfortable.
 o You also have the right to opt out the study at any time, with no consequences.
 o Our team will also share information and resource about on campus and local mental health clinics for youth. If you feel very upset, please reach out to professional resources directly. Our research team is also available to connect you with them whenever needed.

Psychological Risk -- Time Burden

• The time demands of this study are relatively limited. Each EMA survey is designed to take fewer than two minutes to complete, and participants receive approximately four survey prompts per day. This amounts to less than eight minutes of active survey time per day, or approximately two to three hours across the full 28-day study period. Before data collection begins, participants are asked to attend a brief onboarding session during which they will receive instructions for installing the study applications and setting up the Garmin device; this session is estimated to take approximately 30-60 minutes. The pre-screening questionnaire, completed prior to onboarding, takes approximately 15 minutes. At the conclusion of the study, participants will complete an end-of-study survey estimated to take approximately 150 minutes (2.5 hours) to complete. This survey represents the single largest discrete time commitment associated with participation and should be considered when evaluating the total time burden of the study.

• Because passive data collection occurs automatically in the background, it does not require active time from participants beyond the initial installation. However, participants may occasionally need to spend brief amounts of time addressing technical issues, restarting applications, or contacting the research team if problems arise. Although each of these tasks is individually brief, their potential recurrence over four weeks means that cumulative time burden may be slightly higher than the daily estimates alone suggest.

• How we minimize:
 o EMA surveys are intentionally brief and are designed to be completed in under two minutes.
 o Passive sensing reduces the need for active participant input beyond initial setup.
 o We will inform you the estimated time of completing the survey packets and daily surveys.
 o We designed the survey platform to be engaging. No more than 10 questions will be shown on each page, and you will be able to see how many percentages of the survey questions you have finished.
 o You also have the right to opt out the study at any time, with no consequences.
Psychological Risk -- Cognitive and Behavioral Burden

• A meaningful source of ongoing burden in this study is the requirement that participants manage study devices and applications over the course of 28 days. Participants must ensure that both mobile applications remain installed and function properly on their smartphones throughout the study period. For participants also wearing the Garmin device, they must incorporate the charging routine into their schedule (usually need for charge for every few days) and remember to put the device back on after each charge. These tasks are not individually demanding, but they require sustained attention and behavioral consistency across four weeks, which may become more difficult as the excitements of participation fades.

• The EMA surveys themselves may contribute to mild fatigue over time. Completing up to four surveys per day across 28 days results in up to 112 total survey prompts. While each survey is brief, the repetitive nature of the assessments particularly questions about mental health symptoms may feel monotonous or inconvenient for some participants, especially when prompts arrive at inopportune times.

• For participants who choose to pause screenshot data collection using the in-app pause function, an additional layer of cognitive-loaded managing responsibility is introduced. These participants must remember to pause the application when desired and to resume it afterward. Forgetting to resume data collection or encountering difficulty doing so may require contact with the research team, adding to the overall burden.

• How we minimize:
 o You are permitted to skip any individual question you do not wish to answer and may withdraw from the study at any time without penalty.
 o The research team is available to provide technical support throughout the study to reduce the effort required to manage study applications independently.
Psychological Risk -- Phone Screen Monitoring

• The primary source of burden in this study relates to privacy and the awareness of monitoring. The screenshot application captures screen content at high frequency, approximately every five seconds while the phone is in use. As a result, participants may become more aware that their digital activity is being recorded, even though data is handled securely. This heightened self-awareness may cause some participants to modify their natural phone use behavior, feel uncomfortable using their phones for personal activities, or experience a general sense of being monitored throughout the study period.

• It is also worth noting that young adults ages 18 to 25 tend to use their phones heavily for personal communication, social media, and other private activities. Because of this, having their screen captured every five seconds may feel more intrusive to them than it would to older adults. The research team recognizes that privacy-related discomfort may therefore be somewhat greater for this age group than for other adult populations.

• How we minimize:
 o To support participant autonomy, you can pause and resume screenshot data collection at any time through the application.
 o Less than one percent of collected screenshots is expected to be viewed manually by trained research staff; the remainder are processed algorithmically.
 o You may request removal of your data from the research database at any time by contacting the research team.
Informational (privacy) Risks:

• There is possibility that personal sensitive information (e.g. accounts numbers) and identifiable information (e.g. face image of self and others) will be captured in screenshots. All screenshots will be de-identified, labeled by your study ID number, instead of your name. However, there is a risk that the personal information in screenshots may re-identify you or other individuals.

• How we minimize:
 o You can pause and resume screenshot data collection at any time through the application.
 o Less than one percent of collected screenshots is expected to be viewed manually by trained research staff; the remainder are processed algorithmically.
 o You may request removal of your data from the research database at any time by contacting the research team.
 o We will give you a study ID number and use that number, not the name, on all data collected. A secure, password-protected file that links your name to your ID will be kept only by the lead researcher and the study coordinators. We follow Texas Christian University IRB rules to keep your data confidential.

• There is a very small risk that your information could be seen by someone not on the study team. There is also a risk of data breach and loss of confidentiality.

• How we minimize:
 o All screenshot data are encrypted during transmission and stored on a secure, password-protected server in compliance with applicable data security standards.
 o Data will be stored on a secure TCU server approved for private data. All computers and files containing data are password protected, encrypted and backed up on secure TCU servers.
 o We carefully monitor access to the image data, allowing viewing only by authorized study personnel on secure computers over a secure network.
 o Screenshots will be viewed only by TCU researchers trained to protect confidentiality.
What does my participation involve in this study?

This study happens online, with optional in-person visits. Per your preference, you can either come to TCU campus at Winton-Scott Hall in Room 213 or attend a Zoom meeting for the initial screening visit. The study will include the following steps:

1. Onboarding (Room 213 or Zoom)
 • Review the consent form (at the initial visit) and answer any questions.
 • Obtain your consent to participate
 • Help you install the apps on your phone
 • Provide you with a fitness tracker if you are attending in person or information on when to pick it up from Room 213 if on Zoom. We may also ship it to you if you are unable to pick it up for any reason.

2. Questionnaires (online)
 • Complete a 150-minute survey at the beginning of the study
 • Complete brief 2-minute questionnaires four times per day for 28 days
 • Complete a 150-minute survey at the end of the study
 • Some questionnaires ask about stress, difficult life events, executive function, current mood or anxiety, and coping behaviors. You can skip any question you do not want to answer.

3. Fitness Tracker (passively collected)
 • Wear a fitness tracker that records your sleep and activity for 28 days

4. Post-Study Feedback Interview (Room 213 or Zoom)
 • During the study period, you will be asked to share your thoughts on your experience by attending 2 individual and 2 group interviews as well as filling out necessary surveys.

We may learn information about your health as part of the research (for example, mental health). Results are research measures and may not be clinically verified. We will not provide clinical diagnoses or treatment recommendations based on these results.

The Screenomics app will record anything that is on the screen including, for example, home screens, websites, photos, and messages that you send and receive; and collected log data will indicate your real-time location and other information about the applications you use. You will be able to pause the recording or withdraw from the study at any time.

We expect your participation to take 28 days, interacting with research staff once at the beginning and again at the end, if you choose to participate in the feedback interviews.
What rights do I need to obtain to participate?

In order to participate in this project, you must have appropriate rights to share the information described above with the researchers. For example, if your phone screen may display confidential, proprietary or otherwise sensitive or private information of a third party, such as your employer, such third party may prohibit or otherwise object to their participation; or you may have other ethical or legal obligations not to share information on your phone screen with the researchers. By signing below to participate in this research study, you confirm you have obtained, and will maintain during the course of the study, all necessary rights and permissions from third parties to participate and provide the research data to the researchers. Examples of information that you may not have rights to share include but are not limited to: information under attorney-client privilege; proprietary, confidential information belonging to your employer such as emails etc. In addition, you confirm that you are at least 18 years of age, and a resident in the United States.
Are there any alternatives, and how can I withdraw my participation?

You do not have to participate in this research study. You can withdraw by telling a study staff during an interview. We will stop the interview immediately. You can also withdraw by contacting us by email. No reason is required. If you choose to withdraw, we will ask whether you want your study data deleted. If you do, we will remove your data from the dataset and delete it; if you do not, we will keep it, and we will retain it only in a de-identified dataset. We will also ask whether you wish to be considered for future studies. If you agree, we will securely store your name and contact information in a private TCU Box folder and a TCU internal drive; if you decline, we will delete your name and contact information. Because a minimum of 14 days of screenshot data is required to sufficiently estimate a complete 28 days of use, you will be withdrawn from the study if you pause screenshot recording for 14 days in consecutive.
What are the benefits of participating in this study?

Although you will not directly benefit from being in this study, others might benefit because your participation could help researchers better understand how digital technology connects to mental health, which may help professionals better support many young adults.
Will I be compensated for participating in this study?

You will receive compensation of $165 in total for completing all study components, including providing the feedback interviews. If you decide to opt out after the study starts, the compensation you will earn will be calculated based on the tasks finished and the length of participation.

- You will receive a $2.50 electronic gift card for each day of multimodal passive sensing and EMA completion, with bonus incentives of $10 for completing any 14 days and an additional $15 for completing all 28 days of EMA assessments (for a total of up to $95).
- You will also receive $15 for completing the baseline survey and $15 for completing the end-of-epoch survey.
- Thus, you may receive up to $125 for completing the study components above.
- If you also choose to participate in the user-centered feedback interviews and take part in four in-person or virtual meetings to actively engage with the study team and further refine the study protocol, you will receive an additional $10 per meeting.
- You will not be responsible for any costs to participate in this study.

Please inform the researchers if you have any injuries or other health issues related to your participation in the study. You should contact your primary care physician for treatment. If your injury or sickness is an emergency, you should call 911 for an ambulance to take you to the emergency room. You or your insurance will be billed for whatever care you receive. Texas Christian University does not provide compensation or payment for any injury or physical harm that may occur as a result of being in this study. Also, Texas Christian University does not provide compensation for loss of employment, income, or emotional duress that may result from your injury or harm.

By signing this form, you do not give up your right to seek payment if you are harmed as a result of being in this study.
What are my costs to participate in the study?
To participate in the research, you will not need to pay for anything. There will be no additional costs to you as a result of being in this study.
How will my confidentiality be protected?

Every effort will be made to limit the use and disclosure of your personal information, including research study records, to people who have a need to review this information. We cannot promise complete secrecy. Your records may be reviewed by authorized University personnel or other individuals who will be bound by the same provisions of confidentiality.

Most of the data we collect will be analyzed by a computer, but a small portion of the screenshots may be viewed manually by trained TCU researchers (usually less than 1% of collected screenshots). We will not routinely review screenshots while they are collected. Normally, we take all appropriate actions to ensure the security and confidentiality of your data.

However, if participants provide information that suggests a serious concern about their own well-being or the safety of others (including another person communicating with participant) and we detect it, we may need to break confidentiality and share that information with others, including the authorities. We may provide participant referrals for treatment, work with participants to contact their personal physician, trusted family member, or a therapist or work with participants on a plan that may include getting them to a medical facility for safety. It is possible that, based on information gained from this study, the researchers may be obligated to report content required by applicable federal, state, or local laws (e.g., information relating to suicide, physical or sexual abuse) to the appropriate authorities. If a participant is sending/receiving images of drug use or explicit images with another child/adult, this could, in some circumstances, put the sender or receiver at legal risk. If such screenshots were to be captured, this could place participant in unintentional harm. TCU researchers are not in a position to identify or remove such images before they are stored. If sexual assault or harassment is reported or detected with enough specificity to identify potential bad actors within the TCU community, such information will need to be reported to the Title IX Office or the Sexual Harassment Policy Office. Participants' decision whether or not for themselves to participate in this study will not affect participants' employment/medical care.

Your identifiers might be removed from your private records or your samples. Your information or samples could be used and/or distributed to another investigator for future research studies without additional consent from you or your Legally Authorized Representative. All of the data that we gather about your device usage will be kept confidential. We will take precautions to prevent others from learning about your participation in this study. We will not use your name to identify your data file, and the data will be encrypted and stored on a secure TCU server and storage system that will not be accessible to anyone outside of our research project. We will not share your directly identifiable data with anyone outside of the TCU project.
What will happen to the information collected about me after the study is over?

De-identified Screenomics data will be retained for up to 10 years due to the extended timeline required for data collection, processing, analysis, and publication, which often spans multiple years. Retention also supports reproducibility and allows the application of emerging machine learning methods to these high-resolution data, thereby maximizing scientific value. All retained data will be de-identified and stored on secure, institutionally approved systems. Your name and other information that can directly identify you will be kept secure and stored separately from the research data collected as part of the project. De-identified non-screenomic data will be kept indefinitely for future research.\n\nWe may share your research data with other investigators without asking for your consent again, but it will not contain information that could directly identify you.
